title: The Weight-Loss Drugs Millions Take May Be Quietly Dulling Their Sense of Smell and Taste
excerpt: A study of 900,000 patients found GLP-1 users faced an 81% higher risk of smell disturbances — a side effect nobody was tracking.
body:
The weight-loss drugs that have become the most talked-about medications on the planet may come with a sensory side effect that nobody is talking about: they can blunt your ability to smell and taste.

A study of nearly 900,000 patients with type 2 diabetes, published this week in *JAMA Otolaryngology–Head & Neck Surgery*, found that long-term users of GLP-1 receptor agonists — the class of drugs that includes Ozempic, Mounjaro and Wegovy — had an **81 per cent higher risk** of developing smell disturbances and a **52 per cent higher risk** of taste disturbances compared with patients taking other diabetes medications.

The research, led by Jonathan Zontag and Nir Zontag at Hebrew University in Jerusalem, drew on electronic health records from more than 170 healthcare centres worldwide, collected between 2017 and 2026. It is the largest study to date on GLP-1 drugs and sensory function.

## The Numbers Are Small — but the Signal Is Not

In absolute terms, the rates were low: 0.37 per cent of GLP-1 users developed a smell or taste disorder, versus 0.22 per cent of the control group. But in a population of tens of millions of users globally, even a small percentage translates into a large number of people.

The conditions flagged include anosmia (partial or total loss of smell), parosmia (a distorted sense of smell, where familiar scents turn foul or chemical), and parageusia (a distorted sense of taste, or phantom flavours appearing unprompted).

An editorial published alongside the study in *JAMA* put it in human terms. Smell and taste, the editors wrote, shape "the way in which we experience travel, family gatherings, milestones, and the family dinner." GLP-1 drugs that alter "the sensory world that surrounds eating" may diminish something deeper than appetite.

## Why This May Happen

The researchers noted that GLP-1 receptors are widely expressed in the nervous system — both centrally and peripherally. The drugs were designed to mimic the gut hormone GLP-1 to regulate appetite and blood sugar, but their reach extends to areas of the brain involved in sensory processing.

Smell dysfunction, the editorial added, is also "one of the most reliable warning signs of neurodegenerative conditions," making it a marker that clinicians should not dismiss lightly.

## What This Means for Indian-Origin Populations

South Asians are among the populations most vulnerable to type 2 diabetes — the disease strikes earlier, at lower body weights, and at higher rates than in Western populations. As GLP-1 prescriptions surge among Indian-Americans and NRIs in the UK, Canada and the Gulf, this finding has particular relevance.

India itself is on the cusp of wider GLP-1 adoption. Novo Nordisk has made semaglutide (Ozempic) available in India, and compounded versions are already circulating in the grey market. For a culture where food is central to every celebration, reunion and homecoming, even a subtle dulling of taste and smell carries an outsized emotional cost.

The editorial urged caution for patients using GLP-1 drugs for "marginal weight loss or cosmetic purposes," suggesting that the risk-benefit equation is different for those managing serious metabolic disease versus those chasing a dress size.

## The Takeaway

The study does not call for anyone to stop their medication. But it does suggest that the conversation around GLP-1 side effects — so far dominated by nausea, "Ozempic face" and gastrointestinal complaints — needs to expand.

"This study highlights the need for closer monitoring and greater public health awareness," the authors wrote. For now, patients noticing changes in how food smells or tastes should mention it to their doctor rather than writing it off as imagination.

*Sources: JAMA Otolaryngology–Head & Neck Surgery (June 2026); Reuters Health; Healthline; Gizmodo*
